text: What is the capital of Morocco?
explanation: Rabat is the administrative and political capital of the Kingdom of Morocco.

text: How many days are there in a week?
explanation: A week has seven days.

text: Which animal is known as the king of the jungle?
explanation: The lion earned the title for its strength and presence, even though it mostly lives on the savannah.

text: How many colours are there in a rainbow?
explanation: Its seven colours are red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.

text: Which planet do we live on?
explanation: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only one known to support life.

text: In which month do Muslims fast?
explanation: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Hijri calendar, and fasting in it is one of the pillars of Islam.

text: What do bees mainly make honey from?
explanation: Bees collect nectar from flowers and turn it into honey inside the hive.

text: How many players does a football team have on the pitch?
explanation: Each team plays with eleven players, including the goalkeeper.

text: What is the largest ocean in the world?
explanation: The Pacific is the largest and deepest ocean, covering about a third of the Earth's surface.

text: On which continent is most of Egypt located?
explanation: Most of Egypt is in north-east Africa; the Sinai Peninsula is in Asia.

text: Which gas do we need to breathe to stay alive?
explanation: The body's cells need oxygen to produce energy.

text: How many legs does a spider have?
explanation: Spiders are arachnids with eight legs, while insects have six.

text: What is the official currency of Saudi Arabia?
explanation: The Saudi riyal is the kingdom's official currency.

text: Which season comes after winter?
explanation: The seasons go winter, spring, summer, autumn.

text: What is 9 × 9?
explanation: Nine times nine is eighty-one.

text: What is the longest river in Africa?
explanation: At about 6,650 km, the Nile is Africa's longest river.

text: Which animal is known as the ship of the desert?
explanation: The camel copes with thirst and heat and can cover long distances across the desert.

text: How many letters are there in the Arabic alphabet?
explanation: The Arabic alphabet has twenty-eight letters, from alif to ya.

text: What is the capital of France?
explanation: Paris is the capital and largest city of France, and home to the Eiffel Tower.

text: Which organ pumps blood around the human body?
explanation: The heart is a muscle that pumps blood around the body through the blood vessels.

text: Who wrote the "Muqaddimah"?
explanation: Ibn Khaldun wrote it in the 14th century and is regarded as a pioneer of sociology.

text: What is the smallest planet in the Solar System?
explanation: Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun (Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006).

text: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
explanation: Au comes from the Latin aurum; Ag is the symbol for silver.

text: In which year was the first FIFA World Cup held?
explanation: The first tournament was played in 1930 in Uruguay, which also won it.

text: What is the highest mountain in the world above sea level?
explanation: Mount Everest, in the Himalayas, rises to about 8,849 metres.

text: How many bones are there in the adult human body?
explanation: An adult skeleton has 206 bones; babies are born with more, some of which fuse as they grow.

text: What is the capital of Canada?
explanation: Ottawa is Canada's capital, although Toronto is its largest city.

text: Who painted the "Mona Lisa"?
explanation: Leonardo da Vinci painted it in the early 16th century; it hangs in the Louvre.

text: What is the largest Arab country by area?
explanation: Algeria is the largest country in both the Arab world and Africa, at about 2.38 million km².

text: What is the fastest land animal?
explanation: The cheetah can reach nearly 110 km/h over short distances.

text: Which gas is most abundant in the Earth's atmosphere?
explanation: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air, oxygen about 21%.

text: In which city is the University of al-Qarawiyyin?
explanation: Founded in Fez by Fatima al-Fihri in 859, it is one of the oldest universities in the world.

text: How many surahs are there in the Quran?
explanation: The Quran has 114 surahs, from Al-Fatiha to An-Nas.

text: Which language does Google recommend first for building Android apps?
explanation: In 2019 Google announced that Android development would be "Kotlin-first".

text: What is the largest planet in the Solar System?
explanation: Jupiter is a gas giant more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined.

text: Who developed the theory of relativity?
explanation: Einstein published special relativity in 1905 and general relativity in 1915.

text: What is the capital of Australia?
explanation: Canberra was chosen as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne.

text: At what temperature does water boil at sea level?
explanation: Pure water boils at 100 °C under normal atmospheric pressure.

text: Which strait separates Morocco from Spain?
explanation: The Strait of Gibraltar links the Mediterranean to the Atlantic and is about 14 km wide at its narrowest.

text: Which is the only mammal capable of true flight?
explanation: Bats are the only mammals that truly fly; flying squirrels only glide.

text: In which year did Tariq ibn Ziyad cross into al-Andalus?
explanation: Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed in 711 the strait that now bears his name: Gibraltar comes from "Jabal Tariq".

text: What is the deepest known point in the oceans?
explanation: The Challenger Deep, in the Mariana Trench in the Pacific, is almost 11 km deep.

text: Who wrote "The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing" (al-jabr)?
explanation: Al-Khwarizmi laid the foundations of algebra, and the word "algorithm" comes from his name.

text: What is the atomic number of carbon?
explanation: A carbon nucleus has 6 protons; 12 is the mass number of its most common isotope.

text: Who wrote the "Book of Optics" (Kitab al-Manazir), which revolutionised optics?
explanation: Ibn al-Haytham showed through experiments that we see because light travels from objects into the eye.

text: Roughly how fast does light travel in a vacuum?
explanation: Light travels at about 299,792 km per second.

text: Which language has the most native speakers in the world?
explanation: Mandarin has the most native speakers; English has the most speakers overall.

text: In which year did Granada, the last Muslim stronghold in al-Andalus, fall?
explanation: Boabdil surrendered Granada in 1492, the same year Christopher Columbus reached the Americas.

text: What is the largest hot desert in the world?
explanation: The Sahara is the largest hot desert; the largest desert of all is Antarctica.

text: What is the smallest country in the world by area?
explanation: Vatican City covers about 0.44 km² in the heart of Rome.

text: Who founded the Idrisid dynasty in Morocco?
explanation: Idris ibn Abdallah founded the Idrisid dynasty in 788, the first independent Muslim state in Morocco.

text: How many chromosomes are there in a human body cell?
explanation: A body (somatic) cell has 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs; a sex cell has 23.

text: Which planet takes the longest to spin once on its axis?
explanation: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to rotate once, longer than its year of 225 days.

text: In which city was the United Nations Charter signed in 1945?
explanation: The Charter was signed in San Francisco on 26 June 1945 and came into force that October.

text: Which gas makes up most of the atmosphere of Mars?
explanation: Mars has a very thin atmosphere made of about 95% carbon dioxide.

text: Who wrote "Nuzhat al-Mushtaq" and drew its famous map of the world?
explanation: Al-Idrisi completed the work in 1154 for King Roger II of Sicily.

text: Which Moroccan traveller wrote the "Rihla" (Tuhfat al-Nuzzar)?
explanation: Born in Tangier in 1304, Ibn Battuta travelled the Muslim world and beyond for nearly thirty years.

text: What is the unit of electric current?
explanation: The ampere measures current, the volt voltage, the ohm resistance and the watt power.

text: In which year did a human first walk on the Moon?
explanation: Apollo 11 landed on the Moon on 20 July 1969, and Neil Armstrong was the first to walk on it.

text: What is the longest bone in the human body?
explanation: The femur (thigh bone) is the longest and strongest bone in the body.

text: What is the characteristic colour of an emerald gemstone?
explanation: Emeralds are precious gemstones prized for their vibrant green colour caused by traces of chromium.

text: How many days are there in a leap year?
explanation: A leap year contains 366 days instead of the usual 365, with an extra day added to February.

text: What is the primary ingredient of traditional hummus?
explanation: Hummus is traditionally made by blending cooked chickpeas with tahini, olive oil and lemon juice.

text: Which planet in our solar system is nicknamed the Red Planet?
explanation: Mars is known as the Red Planet due to the reddish iron oxide prevalent on its surface.

text: How many sides does a hexagon have?
explanation: A hexagon is a geometrical polygon that has exactly six sides and six angles.

text: Which inventor was awarded the first patent for the electric telephone?
explanation: Alexander Graham Bell was officially granted the first US patent for the telephone in 1876.

text: At what temperature in Celsius does pure water freeze at standard sea level?
explanation: Pure water freezes and solidifies into ice at 0 °C under standard atmospheric conditions.

text: Which is the largest ocean on Earth by surface area?
explanation: The Pacific Ocean is the largest ocean in the world, covering more than 30 percent of the Earth.

text: What is the official currency used in Japan?
explanation: The yen has been the official currency of Japan since 1871 and is widely traded globally.

text: Which of these colours is a primary colour in traditional artistic colour theory?
explanation: Blue is one of the three traditional primary colours, alongside red and yellow.

text: Which instrument is used to measure temperature?
explanation: A thermometer is the standard device used to measure temperature accurately.

text: Which grain forms the essential foundation of Japanese sushi?
explanation: Vinegared Japanese short-grain rice is the core component around which all sushi is prepared.

text: In which country are the famous Pyramids of Giza located?
explanation: The ancient Pyramids of Giza and the Sphinx are located on the outskirts of Cairo in Egypt.

text: Which star is closest to planet Earth?
explanation: The Sun is the closest star to Earth, situated at an average distance of about 150 million kilometres.

text: How many interlocking rings are featured on the official Olympic flag?
explanation: The Olympic flag features five interlocking rings that symbolise the unity of the five inhabited continents.

text: What is the official language of Brazil?
explanation: Portuguese is the official and overwhelmingly predominant language spoken in Brazil.

text: Which organ in the human body is primarily responsible for pumping blood?
explanation: The heart is a muscular organ that continuously pumps blood throughout the circulatory system.

text: What is the hardest naturally occurring mineral on the Mohs hardness scale?
explanation: Diamond defines the top value of 10 on the Mohs scale, making it the hardest natural mineral known.

text: What sweet substance do honeybees produce from flower nectar?
explanation: Honey is naturally produced by honeybees from floral nectar and stored in wax honeycombs.

text: How many hours are there in one complete day?
explanation: One complete day is divided into 24 hours, corresponding to one full rotation of the Earth.

text: On which continent is the Sahara Desert located?
explanation: The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world, occupying the northern portion of Africa.

text: What colour is the five-pointed star located in the centre of the Moroccan national flag?
explanation: The flag of Morocco features a red background with a green five-pointed star in the middle.

text: Which gas do humans inhale from the air that is essential for survival?
explanation: Oxygen is taken in by the lungs during breathing to fuel cellular metabolism throughout the body.

text: Which flightless bird is renowned for its excellent swimming ability in cold southern waters?
explanation: Penguins cannot fly in the air, but their wings have evolved into highly efficient flippers for swimming.

text: How many centimetres are there in one metre?
explanation: Under the International System of Units, one metre is composed of exactly 100 centimetres.

text: Which green fruit is the primary ingredient used to make guacamole?
explanation: Guacamole is a classic Mexican dip made predominantly from mashed fresh avocados.

text: From which cardinal direction does the Sun appear to rise each morning?
explanation: The Sun rises in the east due to the eastward rotation of the Earth on its axis.

text: To which biological class of animals does the frog belong?
explanation: Frogs are amphibians, beginning their life cycle in water as tadpoles before maturing into adults.

text: How many minutes are there in one hour?
explanation: One hour is standardized as containing exactly 60 minutes.

text: What is the standard chemical formula for pure water?
explanation: Water consists of two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom, giving the formula H2O.

text: What is the largest living mammal on Earth?
explanation: The blue whale is the largest known mammal to have ever existed, reaching lengths of up to 30 metres.

text: Which musical instrument typically features 88 black and white keys?
explanation: A standard modern acoustic piano features 88 keys covering over seven octaves.

text: Which geometric polygon is defined by having exactly three sides?
explanation: A triangle is the simplest closed two-dimensional polygon, consisting of three straight sides.

text: In which country is the famous white marble mausoleum known as the Taj Mahal located?
explanation: The Taj Mahal is an iconic mausoleum located in Agra, India, built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan.

text: What is the boiling point of pure water in Celsius at standard atmospheric pressure?
explanation: Under standard atmospheric pressure at sea level, pure water boils into steam at 100 °C.

text: Which is the only country in the world whose national flag is neither rectangular nor square?
explanation: Nepal's flag is the world's only non-quadrilateral national flag, consisting of two stacked triangular pennants.

text: Who was the first human to travel into outer space in 1961?
explanation: Yuri Gagarin made history on 12 April 1961 by completing one orbit of the Earth aboard Vostok 1.

text: Which spice, the most expensive in the world by weight, is harvested from a purple flower?
explanation: Saffron is derived from the stigmas of the Crocus sativus flower, requiring tens of thousands of blooms to yield a single kilogram.

text: In which Italian city was the modern pizza, specifically the Margherita, invented?
explanation: Pizza Margherita was created in Naples in 1889 to honour Queen Margherita of Savoy, using toppings matching the Italian flag.

text: Which Swedish inventor created dynamite and founded the world-famous prizes bearing his name?
explanation: Alfred Nobel invented dynamite in 1867 and bequeathed his vast fortune to establish the prestigious Nobel Prizes.

text: Which national tree is featured at the centre of Lebanon's national flag?
explanation: The Cedar of Lebanon stands in the centre of the Lebanese flag, symbolising resilience and immortality.

text: What is the deepest freshwater lake in the world, holding roughly one-fifth of the world's unfrozen surface fresh water?
explanation: Lake Baikal in Siberia plunges to a depth of 1,642 metres, making it both the deepest and oldest lake on Earth.

text: Who discovered penicillin in 1928, opening the era of antibiotics in modern medicine?
explanation: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin accidentally at St Mary's Hospital in London and was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1945.

text: What is the official distance of an athletic marathon, standardised after the 1908 London Olympics?
explanation: The distance of 42.195 km (26 miles 385 yards) was established at the 1908 Games to finish directly in front of the Royal Box.

text: Which country is the historical birthplace of the coffee plant, from which coffee spread globally?
explanation: Coffea arabica originates in the south-western highlands of Ethiopia, from where trade took it across to Yemen and worldwide.

text: Which emperor ordered the construction of the Taj Mahal in Agra, India, during the 17th century?
explanation: Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built the white marble mausoleum in memory of his favourite wife, Mumtaz Mahal.

text: Which tree's leaf is displayed as the central symbol on Canada's national flag?
explanation: The red eleven-pointed maple leaf has been Canada's official national symbol on its flag since 1965.

text: What is the only metallic element that is liquid at standard room temperature and pressure?
explanation: Mercury is the only metal that remains liquid at room temperature; bromine is also liquid but is a non-metal.

text: Who invented the movable-type printing press in Europe around 1440?
explanation: Johannes Gutenberg introduced movable metal type to Europe, sparking a media revolution across the Western world.

text: What is the lowest dry-land elevation on the surface of the Earth relative to sea level?
explanation: The shores of the Dead Sea sit at over 430 metres below sea level, making it the lowest dry land on Earth.

text: Who was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two distinct sciences?
explanation: Marie Curie won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and in Chemistry in 1911 for her groundbreaking work on radioactivity.

text: Which continent is the only one on Earth that does not have any deserts?
explanation: Europe is the only continent with no true climatic desert regions, benefiting from temperate rainfall patterns.

text: Who wrote the classic literary masterpiece 'Don Quixote', widely regarded as the first modern novel?
explanation: Spanish author Miguel de Cervantes published the two volumes of Don Quixote in 1605 and 1615.

text: Which historic Japanese city served as the imperial capital for over a millennium before Tokyo?
explanation: Kyoto served as Japan's imperial capital from 794 until 1868, when the Emperor relocated to Tokyo.

text: What is the chemical name for common table salt used every day in cooking?
explanation: Common table salt is chemically known as sodium chloride (NaCl), composed of equal parts sodium and chlorine ions.

text: How many hearts does an octopus possess?
explanation: An octopus has three hearts: two pump blood through the gills, while the third circulates blood through the rest of the body.

text: Which maritime strait separates the Asian continent from North America?
explanation: The Bering Strait separates Russia's Chukchi Peninsula from Alaska's Seward Peninsula by roughly 82 kilometres.

text: What designation is given to the highest quality olive oil obtained through pure cold mechanical pressing?
explanation: Extra virgin olive oil is cold-pressed without chemical refining, having an acidity level below 0.8% and superior flavour.

text: Which planet in the Solar System rotates almost completely on its side with an axial tilt of about 98 degrees?
explanation: Uranus features an extreme axial tilt of 97.8 degrees, meaning its north and south poles lie where other planets have their equators.

text: In which Spanish city is the famous Alhambra palace complex, a masterpiece of Moorish architecture, located?
explanation: The Alhambra was built by the Nasrid sultans of the Emirate of Granada during the 13th and 14th centuries.

text: Inside what type of fruit pod do the beans used to make chocolate grow on the tree?
explanation: Cocoa beans grow clustered inside thick, fleshy pods (cabosses) directly attached to the trunk and branches of the cacao tree.

text: Who was the very first person to step onto the surface of the Moon in July 1969?
explanation: Apollo 11 commander Neil Armstrong set foot on the lunar surface on 20 July 1969, followed by Buzz Aldrin.

text: What is the smallest internationally recognised independent state in the world by land area?
explanation: Vatican City covers an area of roughly 0.49 square kilometres, completely landlocked inside Rome, Italy.

text: Which internal organ in the human body is uniquely capable of regenerating lost tissue naturally?
explanation: The human liver can fully regenerate its original mass even after surgical removal of up to 70% of its tissue.

text: What are the world's highest uninterrupted waterfalls, located in Venezuela?
explanation: Angel Falls (Salto Ángel) drops 979 metres, with an uninterrupted plunge of 807 metres in Canaima National Park.

text: Who painted the celebrated mural 'The Last Supper' in the convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan?
explanation: Leonardo da Vinci created 'The Last Supper' during the late 15th century for his patron, Duke Ludovico Sforza.

text: What is the fastest land animal in the world over short sprinting distances?
explanation: The cheetah can accelerate from 0 to 100 km/h in roughly three seconds, reaching top speeds of up to 110 km/h.

text: Which rock-cut Nabataean city carved into rose-red cliffs is Jordan's most famous historic site?
explanation: Petra was established by the Nabataeans as their capital and trading hub, famous for structures like the Treasury.

text: What was the original historical name of Rome's Colosseum when it was constructed in antiquity?
explanation: The Colosseum was built by the emperors of the Flavian dynasty (Vespasian and Titus), hence its Roman name, the Flavian Amphitheatre.

text: Which citrus fruit flavour is traditionally added to black tea to create classic Earl Grey tea?
explanation: Earl Grey is a flavoured tea blend infused with oil extracted from the rind of the bergamot orange.

text: Which body part does a snake flick into the air to collect scent particles for its Jacobson's organ?
explanation: Snakes flick their forked tongues to gather airborne chemical particles, delivering them to the sensory Jacobson's organ in the mouth.

text: Which spice is derived from the dried aril (outer lacy coating) of the nutmeg seed?
explanation: Mace is the dried reddish aril surrounding the nutmeg seed and has a subtler, more fragrant aroma.

text: What was the first commercial product ever scanned with a barcode at a retail checkout in 1974?
explanation: A pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit chewing gum was scanned at a supermarket in Ohio on 26 June 1974.

text: Which renowned painter was born in Crete and named Doménikos Theotokópoulos?
explanation: Doménikos Theotokópoulos became universally known as El Greco ('The Greek') during his career in Spain.

text: Which weapon is depicted alongside a book and a hoe on the national flag of Mozambique?
explanation: The flag of Mozambique features an AK-47 assault rifle with bayonet attached, symbolizing national defence.

text: Who is the only person in history to have won two unshared Nobel Prizes?
explanation: Linus Pauling won the 1954 Chemistry Prize and the 1962 Peace Prize as sole recipient for both.

text: Which noble gas derives its name from the Greek word meaning 'stranger'?
explanation: Xenon takes its name from the Greek word 'xenos', meaning stranger or foreign.

text: The Italian liqueur Amaretto is traditionally primarily flavoured with the kernels of which fruit?
explanation: Amaretto liqueur is traditionally flavoured primarily using apricot stone kernels, which contain benzaldehyde.

text: Who invented and patented the first mechanical cash register in 1879?
explanation: Saloon keeper James Ritty invented the first mechanical cash register in 1879 to prevent employee pilfering.

text: How many stars make up the Southern Cross depicted on the national flag of New Zealand?
explanation: New Zealand's flag displays 4 red stars with white borders representing the Southern Cross constellation.

text: In traditional Japanese Kabuki theatre, what is the term for male actors who specialise in playing female roles?
explanation: Onnagata are male actors who specialize in female roles in the all-male tradition of Kabuki theatre.

text: Which astronaut remained in lunar orbit piloting the command module during the Apollo 11 Moon landing?
explanation: Michael Collins piloted the command module Columbia in lunar orbit while Armstrong and Aldrin walked on the Moon.

text: What is the specific name for the small plastic or metal sheath at the end of a shoelace?
explanation: An aglet is the small sheath fitted onto each end of a shoelace to keep the fibres from fraying.

text: The Middle Eastern baking spice 'mahlab' is produced by grinding the seed kernels of which tree?
explanation: Mahlab is made from the ground inner kernels of the cherry stones of the St Lucie cherry (Prunus mahaleb).

text: Which French engineer co-invented the modern scuba diving regulator with Jacques Cousteau in 1943?
explanation: Émile Gagnan adapted a gas regulator for diving use, co-patenting the Aqua-Lung with Jacques Cousteau.

text: Which ancient library in Asia Minor rivalled the Library of Alexandria and gave its name to parchment?
explanation: The Library of Pergamum was Alexandria's main rival; parchment takes its name directly from the city.

text: Which mythological creature is depicted in the centre of the national flag of Bhutan?
explanation: The flag of Bhutan features Druk, the white Thunder Dragon, holding jewels representing national wealth.

text: What was the radio call sign of Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman in space, during her 1963 flight?
explanation: Valentina Tereshkova communicated using the call sign Chaika ('Seagull') aboard Vostok 6 in June 1963.

text: According to strict protected designation rules, authentic Roquefort cheese must be produced from the milk of which animal?
explanation: Authentic French Roquefort blue cheese must legally be made exclusively from raw sheep's (ewe's) milk.

text: What is the exact international standard length of one nautical mile in metres?
explanation: The international nautical mile was standardized in 1929 as exactly 1,852 metres.

text: Who invented the first handheld mobile cellular phone while leading the team at Motorola in 1973?
explanation: Martin Cooper placed the first public handheld mobile phone call from a Manhattan street on 3 April 1973.

text: In ancient Roman public baths, what was the Latin name of the room containing the hot plunge bath?
explanation: The caldarium was the hot room in a Roman bath complex, heated from below by an underfloor hypocaust system.

text: The national flag of the Philippines is unique in being flown with its red stripe on top under which circumstance?
options: When the country is in a state of war
explanation: By Philippine law, displaying the flag with the red stripe uppermost signals that the nation is in a state of war.

text: Who was the first person to complete a single-handed, non-stop circumnavigation of the world by boat in 1969?
explanation: Sir Robin Knox-Johnston won the Sunday Times Golden Globe Race in 1969 aboard his ketch Suhaili.

text: What gives traditional absinthe its distinctive green colour during natural secondary maceration?
explanation: The pale green tint of traditional absinthe is derived from chlorophyll released by herbs steeped after distillation.

text: What is the technical term for the wire cage fitted over the cork of a sparkling wine or champagne bottle?
explanation: A muselet is the wire cage designed to prevent the cork from blowing out under high internal carbonation pressure.

text: Which American inventor developed the first commercial typewriter and devised the QWERTY keyboard layout?
explanation: Christopher Latham Sholes devised the QWERTY layout in the 1870s to minimize jamming of physical typebars.

text: What is the traditional name of the wooden chest decorated with brass studs historically used in the Gulf?
explanation: A mandoos is an ornate, brass-studded wooden chest traditionally used across the Arabian Gulf to protect valuables.

text: Which constellation is depicted at the centre of the blue celestial sphere on the flag of Brazil?
explanation: The Southern Cross (Crux) sits at the centre of the blue disc, representing the sky over Rio on 15 November 1889.

text: What was the name of the monoplane flown by Charles Lindbergh on the first solo non-stop transatlantic flight?
explanation: Lindbergh named his custom Ryan monoplane 'Spirit of St. Louis' after the Missouri city of his financial backers.

text: Kopi Luwak, one of the world's most expensive coffees, is processed through the digestive tract of which animal?
explanation: The Asian palm civet feeds on coffee cherries, excreting the beans after enzymes partially ferment them in its gut.

text: On a standard European roulette wheel, what is the sum of all the numbers from 0 to 36?
explanation: Adding every number on a roulette wheel from 1 to 36 yields 666, fueling the urban myth of the 'Devil's Wheel'.

text: Which inventor designed and demonstrated the first safety elevator with an automatic brake in 1853?
explanation: Elisha Otis dramatically demonstrated his safety elevator mechanism at the 1854 New York World's Fair.

text: What does the Arabic name 'Al-Khazneh', given to the famous rock-cut facade in Petra, mean?
explanation: Al-Khazneh translates to 'The Treasury', stemming from a local legend that bandits concealed wealth in its top urn.

text: Besides Vatican City, which is the only sovereign country in the world to have an officially square flag?
explanation: Switzerland and Vatican City are the only two sovereign states that have officially square (1:1 aspect ratio) flags.

text: Which Spanish navigator completed the first single-voyage circumnavigation of the globe in 1522?
explanation: Juan Sebastián Elcano took command of the ship Victoria after Magellan died in the Philippines, completing the voyage.

text: Which spice is made from the dried stigmas of Crocus sativus and requires 75,000 flowers per pound?
explanation: Saffron is the world's costliest spice by weight because each fragile crimson stigma must be harvested by hand.

text: What is the official standard inner diameter of a regulation basketball rim in NBA and FIBA rules?
explanation: The inner diameter of a regulation basketball rim is exactly 18 inches (45.72 cm), wide enough to fit two balls.

text: Which American researcher developed the first successful inactivated polio vaccine, declared safe in 1955?
explanation: Dr Jonas Salk developed the injected inactivated polio vaccine and famously refused to patent it for private profit.

text: What is the Japanese art of repairing broken pottery with lacquer dusted with powdered gold called?
explanation: Kintsugi ('golden joinery') is the philosophy of treating breakage and repair as part of the object's history.

text: Which spice is depicted inside the yellow hoist triangle of the national flag of Grenada?
explanation: Grenada is known as the 'Isle of Spice', and its flag features a stylized nutmeg clove within the hoist triangle.

text: What is the largest organ of the human body?
explanation: Skin is the human body's largest organ, serving as a protective outer barrier.

text: Which gas do plants absorb from the air to perform photosynthesis?
explanation: Plants take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen during the process of photosynthesis.

text: What is the force that pulls objects towards the centre of the Earth?
explanation: Gravity is the fundamental force responsible for drawing objects towards the Earth's centre.

text: What is the only natural satellite of the Earth?
explanation: The Moon is Earth's sole permanent natural satellite.

text: What is the sum of the interior angles of a flat triangle?
explanation: In standard Euclidean geometry, the internal angles of any triangle always add up to 180 degrees.

text: To which class of animals do bees and ants belong?
explanation: Bees and ants are classified as insects, characterised by six legs and a segmented body.

text: Which of these travels faster through the air?
explanation: Light travels at roughly 300,000 kilometres per second, far outstripping the speed of sound.

text: What is the square root of the number 64?
explanation: The square root of 64 is 8, because 8 multiplied by 8 equals 64.

text: At what temperature on the Celsius scale does pure water freeze?
explanation: Pure water transitions from liquid to solid ice at 0 degrees Celsius.

text: Which part of the human eye gives it its colour?
explanation: The iris is the pigmented circular structure that controls pupil size and eye colour.

text: Which blood cells are primarily responsible for fighting infections?
explanation: White blood cells are an essential part of the immune system that combats pathogens and disease.

text: Which planet in the Solar System takes longer to rotate on its axis than to complete an orbit around the Sun?
explanation: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to complete one rotation on its axis, while its orbital period around the Sun is only 225 Earth days.

text: Which of these subatomic particles carries no electrical charge?
explanation: The neutron has a neutral electrical charge and resides inside the atomic nucleus alongside positively charged protons.

text: Which cellular organelle is often referred to as the powerhouse of the cell?
explanation: Mitochondria generate most of the chemical energy needed to power the cell's biochemical reactions in the form of ATP.

text: What is the only prime number that is also an even number?
explanation: The number 2 is the smallest prime number and the only even one, as all other even numbers are divisible by 2.

text: What physical phenomenon causes a straw to appear bent when placed in a glass of water?
explanation: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes between media of different densities, such as air and water, due to a change in speed.

text: Which blood type is considered the universal donor for red blood cells?
explanation: O negative red blood cells lack A, B, and Rh antigens, making them safe for transfusion to virtually any recipient.

text: Which major spiral galaxy is closest to our Milky Way galaxy?
explanation: The Andromeda Galaxy is roughly 2.5 million light-years away and is the largest member of our Local Group.

text: Which chemical element is represented by the symbol 'Fe' in the periodic table?
explanation: The chemical symbol Fe is derived from the Latin word 'ferrum', meaning iron.

text: What green pigment in plants is responsible for absorbing light during photosynthesis?
explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs blue and red wavelengths while reflecting green light, giving plants their characteristic colour.

text: What is the geometric name for a polygon with five sides?
explanation: A pentagon has five sides and five angles, with interior angles that always sum up to 540 degrees.

text: What is the hardest biological substance produced by the human body?
explanation: Tooth enamel contains over 95% mineral content, primarily hydroxyapatite, making it harder than bone.

text: Which English scientist formulated the three classical laws of motion?
explanation: Sir Isaac Newton published his three universal laws of motion in his foundational 1687 work, the Principia.

text: What is the pH value of pure water at a temperature of 25 degrees Celsius?
explanation: A pH of 7 represents a completely neutral solution where hydrogen and hydroxide ions exist in equal concentrations.

text: What is the scientific term for the boundary of a black hole beyond which nothing can escape?
explanation: The event horizon is the boundary where the gravitational pull becomes so strong that even light cannot escape.

text: Which part of the human brain is primarily responsible for balance and muscle coordination?
explanation: The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movements, motor learning, and maintains physical balance and posture.

text: What is the value of the mathematical constant pi rounded to two decimal places?
explanation: Pi represents the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, approximately equal to 3.14159.

text: Which type of electromagnetic radiation has the shortest wavelength and the highest energy?
explanation: Gamma rays have the highest frequency and shortest wavelength in the electromagnetic spectrum, carrying tremendous energy.

text: What is the largest natural satellite (moon) in the Solar System?
explanation: Ganymede, which orbits Jupiter, is the largest moon in the Solar System, being even larger in diameter than the planet Mercury.

text: In biology, what does the abbreviation DNA stand for?
explanation: Deoxyribonucleic acid is the polymer that carries genetic instructions used in growth, development, functioning, and reproduction.

text: How many chambers are there in the human heart?
explanation: The human heart consists of four chambers: the right and left atria on top, and the right and left ventricles below.

text: What unit of measurement is used for electrical resistance?
explanation: The ohm is named after the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm, who developed the relationship between voltage and current.

text: Which hydrocarbon gas is the primary component of natural gas?
explanation: Methane (CH4) typically makes up 70% to 90% of raw natural gas extracted from the ground.

text: What is the name of a triangle whose three sides are all equal in length?
explanation: An equilateral triangle has three sides of equal length and three equal interior angles of 60 degrees each.

text: Which outer atmospheric layer of the Sun is prominently visible during a total solar eclipse?
explanation: The corona is the Sun's outermost atmosphere, appearing as a pearly white halo during a total solar eclipse.

text: What anaerobic biological process do yeast cells perform to convert sugars into alcohol and carbon dioxide?
explanation: Fermentation is an anaerobic metabolic pathway in which yeast breaks down sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide.

text: Which hormone produced by the pancreas lowers glucose levels in the bloodstream?
explanation: Insulin is secreted by beta cells in the pancreas to enable cells to absorb glucose from the blood for energy.

text: Approximately what is the speed of sound in dry air at 20 degrees Celsius?
explanation: In dry air at 20 degrees Celsius, sound travels at approximately 343 metres per second (around 1,235 km/h).

text: Which gas turns limewater cloudy when bubbled through it?
explanation: Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide in limewater to produce an insoluble white precipitate of calcium carbonate.

text: What is the sum of the interior angles of any convex quadrilateral?
explanation: A quadrilateral can be split into two triangles, and since each contains 180 degrees, the interior angles sum to 360 degrees.

text: What is the disc-shaped region of icy bodies situated beyond the orbit of Neptune?
explanation: The Kuiper Belt extends from Neptune's orbit outwards, containing millions of icy objects and dwarf planets such as Pluto.

text: What type of biological relationship occurs when one organism benefits at the expense of harm to the host?
explanation: Parasitism is a symbiotic relationship where the parasite derives nutrients or shelter while harming the host organism.

text: Which fundamental physical force keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
explanation: Gravity is the attractive force that acts between masses, keeping planets locked in orbital paths around the Sun.

text: What is the chemical formula for ordinary table salt?
explanation: Table salt is composed of sodium chloride, an ionic compound formed from sodium and chlorine in a 1:1 ratio.

text: In a right-angled triangle, what is the side opposite the right angle called?
explanation: The hypotenuse is the longest side of a right-angled triangle and lies directly across from the 90-degree right angle.

text: Approximately how long does it take for sunlight to travel to Earth?
explanation: Travelling at roughly 300,000 kilometres per second, sunlight covers the 150 million kilometres to Earth in about 8 minutes and 20 seconds.

text: What is the maximum theoretical mass of a stable white dwarf star, known as the Chandrasekhar limit?
explanation: The Chandrasekhar limit is approximately 1.44 solar masses; beyond this mass, electron degeneracy pressure cannot prevent collapse.

text: Which standard start codon in the genetic code codes for the amino acid methionine?
explanation: The codon AUG serves as the universal initiation signal for protein synthesis and encodes methionine.

text: Which cranial nerve is the longest in the human body, extending to the thorax and abdomen?
explanation: The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) extends from the brainstem down through the neck, thorax, and into the abdomen.

text: Which mathematician successfully proved Fermat's Last Theorem over 350 years after it was proposed?
explanation: British mathematician Andrew Wiles published the definitive proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in 1995.

text: Which cellular organelle possesses its own circular DNA and serves as the primary site of oxidative phosphorylation?
explanation: The mitochondrion retains its own circular genome and generates most of the chemical energy needed by the cell.

text: What is the SI derived unit of magnetic flux?
explanation: The weber (Wb) is the SI unit of magnetic flux, whereas the tesla measures magnetic flux density.

text: Which chemical element has the highest melting point among all pure metals?
explanation: Tungsten has a melting point of approximately 3,422 °C (6,192 °F), higher than any other pure metal.

text: Which enzyme is responsible for unwinding the DNA double helix during replication?
explanation: Helicases break the hydrogen bonds between nucleotide base pairs to unwind the DNA double helix.

text: Which moon of Saturn is famous for geysers of water ice erupting from its south polar region?
explanation: Enceladus harbours a subsurface liquid ocean that feeds cryovolcanic plumes detected by the Cassini spacecraft.

text: Which Millennium Prize Problem was solved by Russian mathematician Grigori Perelman in 2003?
explanation: Grigori Perelman proved the Poincaré conjecture using Ricci flow with surgery, famously declining the prize money.

text: Which gauge boson is the mediator of the strong force that binds quarks together inside hadrons?
explanation: Gluons act as the exchange particles for the strong colour force between quarks in quantum chromodynamics.

text: Which region of the human brain synthesises the dopamine that is crucial for motor control?
explanation: The substantia nigra in the midbrain produces dopamine; loss of its dopaminergic neurons leads to Parkinson's disease.

text: What is the primary metal catalyst traditionally used in the Haber-Bosch process to synthesize ammonia?
explanation: The Haber-Bosch process uses iron-based catalysts promoted with potassium oxide to synthesize ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.

text: What is the approximate effective surface temperature of the Sun's photosphere in kelvins?
explanation: The solar photosphere has an effective temperature of approximately 5,778 K, emitting yellow-white light.

text: In the Krebs cycle, which molecule condenses with oxaloacetate to form citrate?
explanation: Acetyl-CoA condenses with oxaloacetate in the initial step of the citric acid cycle, catalysed by citrate synthase.

text: Which physicist experimentally discovered the positron in 1932 using a cloud chamber?
explanation: Carl Anderson confirmed Dirac's theoretical prediction by detecting positron tracks produced by cosmic rays in 1932.

text: What is the geometric name of the regular polyhedron that has 20 equilateral triangular faces?
explanation: An icosahedron is one of the five Platonic solids, featuring 20 equilateral triangular faces and 12 vertices.

text: Which hormone is produced by the parafollicular cells (C cells) of the thyroid gland to lower blood calcium levels?
explanation: Calcitonin is secreted by thyroid C cells and acts antagonistically to parathyroid hormone to decrease blood calcium.

text: Which gas law states that the pressure of a given mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature at constant volume?
explanation: Gay-Lussac's law dictates that P is directly proportional to T (in kelvins) when volume is held constant.

text: What relativistic effect describes the reduction in frequency of electromagnetic radiation climbing out of a gravitational well?
explanation: Gravitational redshift occurs because photons expend energy to escape a gravitational field, shifting towards longer wavelengths.

text: What vascular plant tissue is primarily responsible for transporting water and dissolved inorganic minerals upward from roots?
explanation: Xylem transports water and dissolved nutrients upwards, whereas phloem distributes sugars manufactured by photosynthesis.

text: What type of epithelium lines the inner surface of the human trachea?
explanation: The respiratory epithelium lining the trachea is pseudostratified ciliated columnar, assisting in mucociliary clearance.

text: What is the oxidation state of the oxygen atoms in hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)?
explanation: In peroxides like H2O2, each oxygen atom possesses an oxidation number of -1 due to the single O-O bond.

text: Which mathematical constant represents the limiting difference between the harmonic series and the natural logarithm?
explanation: The Euler-Mascheroni constant (denoted by gamma, γ) is defined as the limit of the sum of 1/k minus ln(n) as n approaches infinity.

text: What is the name of the hypothetical spherical cloud of predominantly icy planetesimals surrounding the Solar System?
explanation: The Oort cloud is considered the vast reservoir for long-period comets, lying far beyond Pluto and the Kuiper belt.

text: Which quantum mechanical principle asserts that two identical fermions cannot occupy the same quantum state simultaneously?
explanation: Formulated by Wolfgang Pauli in 1925, this principle governs electron shell configurations and the stability of matter.

text: Which spirochete genus of bacteria is the causative agent of tick-borne Lyme disease?
explanation: Lyme disease is primarily caused by Borrelia burgdorferi and transmitted to humans via bites from infected blacklegged ticks.

text: What is the anatomical name for the large opening in the occipital bone through which the spinal cord enters the skull?
explanation: The foramen magnum is the large oval opening in the base of the skull providing passage for the spinal cord and vertebral arteries.

text: Which noble gas is naturally radioactive and is formed directly from the radioactive decay of radium?
explanation: Radon is a radioactive, colourless noble gas produced along the uranium decay series, posing environmental health risks.

text: What physical quantity is the reciprocal of electrical resistance and is measured in siemens?
explanation: Conductance (symbol G) quantifies how easily electric current flows through a conductor and equals the inverse of resistance.

text: In number theory, what is a prime number called that can be written in the form 2^p - 1?
explanation: A Mersenne prime takes the form 2^p - 1; each known Mersenne prime corresponds directly to an even perfect number.

text: What is the densest known type of stellar remnant in the universe that has not collapsed into a black hole?
explanation: A neutron star packs upwards of 1.4 solar masses into a sphere merely 20 kilometres across, supported by neutron degeneracy.

text: Which immunoglobulin class is the most abundant in human serum and the only one that can cross the placenta?
explanation: Immunoglobulin G (IgG) constitutes about 75-80% of human antibodies and confers passive humoral immunity to the fetus.

text: What is the molecular geometry of sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) according to VSEPR theory?
explanation: Sulfur hexafluoride has six single bonds and zero lone pairs on the central sulfur atom, resulting in an octahedral shape.

text: What cylindrical organelle consists of nine triplets of microtubules arranged in a ring to organise the mitotic spindle?
explanation: Centrioles display a characteristic 9-triplet microtubule cylinder structure and organize the centrosome in animal cells.

text: What physical phenomenon produces a transverse voltage across an electrical conductor carrying a current in a magnetic field?
explanation: Discovered by Edwin Hall in 1879, the Hall effect is fundamental in sensing magnetic fields and semiconductor characterisation.

text: What is the exact defined speed of light in a vacuum in metres per second according to the SI standard?
explanation: The speed of light in vacuum (c) is defined as exactly 299,792,458 m/s, fixing the definition of the SI metre.

text: Who was the first Rashidun caliph in Islamic history?
explanation: Abu Bakr became the first caliph in 632 following the death of the Prophet Muhammad, ruling until 634.

text: In which year did Christopher Columbus reach the Americas?
explanation: Columbus reached the Bahamas in October 1492 on an expedition sponsored by the Spanish monarchs.

text: Which military leader was crowned Emperor of the French in 1804?
explanation: Napoleon Bonaparte crowned himself Emperor of the French at Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris in 1804.

text: Which city served as the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate?
explanation: Caliph Abu Ja'far al-Mansur founded Baghdad in 762 to serve as the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate.

text: What was the name of the famous ship that sank on its maiden voyage in 1912?
explanation: The Titanic sank in the North Atlantic Ocean after hitting an iceberg in April 1912.

text: Which leader founded the Mongol Empire?
explanation: Genghis Khan united nomadic tribes in 1206 to found one of the largest contiguous empires in history.

text: Who was the first President of the United States?
explanation: George Washington served as the first American president from 1789 to 1797.

text: Which Muslim commander led the conquest of Andalusia in 711 AD?
explanation: Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed the strait named after him in 711 AD to begin the conquest of the Iberian Peninsula.

text: In which city was the Prophet Muhammad born?
explanation: The Prophet Muhammad was born in Mecca in the Year of the Elephant, around 570 AD.

text: Which ancient civilisation built the citadel of Machu Picchu in Peru?
explanation: The Inca Empire constructed Machu Picchu high in the Andes mountains during the 15th century.

text: In which year did the Second World War end?
explanation: The Second World War concluded with the official surrender of Japan in September 1945.

text: Which South African leader spent 27 years in prison fighting apartheid?
explanation: Nelson Mandela was released in 1990 and became South Africa's first Black president in 1994.

text: Which Ottoman sultan was known in the West as 'the Magnificent'?
explanation: Suleiman the Magnificent ruled the Ottoman Empire at its height from 1520 to 1566.

text: Which European capital was divided by a famous wall that fell in 1989?
explanation: The Berlin Wall separated the city from 1961 until its historic fall in November 1989.

text: What is the name of the Moroccan traveller who explored the medieval world in the 14th century?
explanation: Ibn Battuta left his hometown of Tangier in 1325 and travelled for roughly thirty years across Afro-Eurasia.

text: Who was the last Ptolemaic ruler of Egypt before it became a Roman province?
explanation: Cleopatra VII died in 30 BC following her defeat alongside Mark Antony, ending Ptolemaic rule.

text: In which year did the French Revolution begin with the storming of the Bastille?
explanation: The storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789 marked the outbreak of the French Revolution.

text: Which Muslim dynasty ruled al-Andalus and made Cordoba their capital?
explanation: Abd al-Rahman I established the Umayyad Emirate in Cordoba in 756 following the fall of Damascus.

text: Who was the first astronaut to walk on the Moon in 1969?
explanation: Neil Armstrong stepped onto the lunar surface on 20 July 1969 during the Apollo 11 mission.

text: Which Muslim leader recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187?
explanation: Saladin recaptured Jerusalem in 1187 following his victory over the Crusaders at the Battle of Hattin.

text: Which ancient Greek philosopher was the personal tutor of Alexander the Great?
explanation: Aristotle was hired by King Philip II of Macedon to educate his young son Alexander.

text: In which European country did the Renaissance movement begin?
explanation: The Renaissance began in the Italian city-states, most notably Florence, before spreading across Europe.

text: Which capital of the Byzantine Empire was conquered by the Ottomans in 1453?
explanation: Constantinople fell to the Ottoman forces in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire.

text: In which year did the First World War break out?
explanation: The First World War began in 1914 following the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria.

text: Who delivered the famous 'I Have a Dream' speech in 1963?
explanation: Martin Luther King Jr. gave the historic speech during the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.

text: Which ancient civilisation built the famous Colosseum?
explanation: The Colosseum was built by the Romans under the Flavian dynasty in the first century AD.

text: What was the name of the grand intellectual centre and library in Abbasid Baghdad?
explanation: The House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma) was a renowned translation centre and library in Baghdad.

text: Which decisive battle took place in 1066, reshaping the history of England?
explanation: William the Conqueror won the Battle of Hastings in 1066, securing the Norman conquest of England.

text: Which Almoravid leader founded the city of Marrakech as his imperial capital?
explanation: Yusuf ibn Tashfin established Marrakech around 1070 as the capital of the Almoravid Empire.

text: Which female scientist won two Nobel Prizes in two different scientific fields?
explanation: Marie Curie won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911.

text: Along the banks of which river did ancient Egyptian civilisation flourish?
explanation: The annual flooding of the Nile provided fertile soil that sustained ancient Egyptian civilisation.

text: Which Ottoman sultan conquered the city of Constantinople in 1453?
explanation: Mehmed II earned the title 'the Conqueror' after taking Constantinople at the age of just 21.

text: Which country was ruled by tsars of the Romanov dynasty until 1917?
explanation: The 1917 Russian Revolution brought an end to Tsar Nicholas II and the Romanov dynasty.

text: Which country gifted the Statue of Liberty to the United States in 1886?
explanation: France gifted the statue to commemorate the centennial of the US Declaration of Independence.

text: Which Muslim physician and philosopher, known in the West as Avicenna, wrote 'The Canon of Medicine'?
explanation: Ibn Sina wrote 'The Canon of Medicine', which remained a standard medical textbook in Europe for centuries.

text: For which pharaoh was the Great Pyramid of Giza constructed?
explanation: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built for Pharaoh Khufu during Egypt's Fourth Dynasty.

text: Which ancient writing system developed in Mesopotamia used wedge-shaped marks?
explanation: Cuneiform was invented by the Sumerians in Mesopotamia around 3200 BC using reeds on clay tablets.

text: Who was the first Roman emperor, previously known as Octavian?
explanation: Augustus became the first Roman emperor in 27 BC, marking the transition from Republic to Empire.

text: Which is the oldest continually operating university in the world, founded by Fatima al-Fihri in Fez?
explanation: The University of al-Qarawiyyin was founded in 859 AD in Fez and is recognised by UNESCO as the world's oldest university.

text: In which year did Constantinople fall to the Ottoman Empire under Sultan Mehmed II?
explanation: Constantinople fell in 1453, bringing an end to the Byzantine Empire after a 53-day siege.

text: Who was the very first emperor of the Roman Empire?
explanation: Augustus, originally named Octavian, became the first Roman emperor in 27 BC following the fall of the Roman Republic.

text: In which famous battle did Saladin defeat the Crusader forces in 1187?
explanation: The Battle of Hattin in July 1187 broke the Crusader power in the Levant and led directly to the recapture of Jerusalem.

text: Which Abbasid Caliph founded the city of Baghdad to serve as his capital?
explanation: Caliph Abu Ja'far al-Mansur founded Baghdad in 762 AD, designating it as the Round City or City of Peace.

text: In which country did the Battle of Alcácer Quibir (Battle of the Three Kings) take place in 1578?
explanation: Fought near Ksar El Kebir in northern Morocco, it resulted in the death of King Sebastian of Portugal and two Moroccan claimants.

text: In which year was the Magna Carta signed in England?
explanation: King John of England was forced by his barons to grant the Magna Carta at Runnymede in June 1215.

text: Which commander led the Muslim army at the pivotal Battle of al-Qadisiyyah against the Sasanian Empire?
explanation: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas commanded the Muslim forces in 636 AD, resulting in a decisive victory over the Sasanian Empire.

text: Which Carthaginian general famously crossed the Alps with war elephants to invade Rome?
explanation: Hannibal led his army and war elephants across the Alps in 218 BC during the Second Punic War.

text: In which year did the Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula (al-Andalus) begin?
explanation: Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed into Iberia in 711 AD, defeating the Visigothic king Roderic at the Battle of Guadalete.

text: In which year did the Berlin Wall fall, opening the way to German reunification?
explanation: The Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989 following widespread civil protests across East Germany.

text: Which Mamluk sultan led the Muslim forces to defeat the Mongols at the Battle of Ain Jalut in 1260?
explanation: Sultan Saif al-Din Qutuz led the Mamluk army to victory at Ain Jalut, halting the Mongol advance into Egypt.

text: Which Mughal Emperor commissioned the building of the Taj Mahal in memory of his wife?
explanation: Shah Jahan commissioned the Taj Mahal in Agra following the death of his favourite wife, Mumtaz Mahal.

text: In which year was the Suez Canal officially opened for international navigation?
explanation: The Suez Canal was officially opened on 17 November 1869 during the reign of Khedive Ismail of Egypt.

text: Which peace treaty brought an end to the Thirty Years' War in Europe in 1648?
explanation: The Peace of Westphalia established the principle of national sovereignty and reshaped the political map of Europe in 1648.

text: The rock-carved ancient city of Petra was the capital of which civilisation?
explanation: Petra, located in modern-day Jordan, served as the capital of the Arab Nabataean Kingdom from the 4th century BC.

text: Which French monarch, known as the 'Sun King', had the longest verified reign in history?
explanation: Louis XIV ruled France for over 72 years, from 1643 until his death in 1715, building the Palace of Versailles.

text: Which battle marked the final military defeat of Napoleon Bonaparte in 1815?
explanation: Fought in present-day Belgium in June 1815, the Battle of Waterloo resulted in Napoleon's permanent exile to Saint Helena.

text: Who discovered the nearly intact tomb of Pharaoh Tutankhamun in the Valley of the Kings in 1922?
explanation: British archaeologist Howard Carter made the world-famous discovery of King Tutankhamun's tomb in November 1922.

text: Which famed Moroccan explorer set out from Tangier in the 14th century to travel across the known world?
explanation: Ibn Battuta travelled over 70,000 miles across Africa, the Middle East, India, and China over a span of thirty years.

text: Which ancient civilisation is associated with King Hammurabi and his famous legal code?
explanation: Hammurabi was the sixth king of the First Babylonian Dynasty, best known for the Code of Hammurabi inscribed c. 1754 BC.

text: In which century did the Black Death devastate Europe, Asia, and North Africa?
explanation: The Black Death struck in the mid-14th century (peaking between 1347 and 1351), killing tens of millions of people.

text: What ancient name did the Romans give to the region that roughly corresponds to modern-day France?
explanation: The Romans called the territory Gaul, which was conquered by Julius Caesar during the Gallic Wars between 58 and 50 BC.

text: Which artefact found in 1799 allowed scholars to decipher ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs?
explanation: Discovered near Rashid (Rosetta), the trilingual inscription enabled Jean-François Champollion to decode Egyptian hieroglyphs.

text: Who was the British Prime Minister during the majority of the Second World War?
explanation: Winston Churchill led the United Kingdom as Prime Minister from May 1940 to July 1945.

text: In which city was the 1884–1885 conference held that formalised the European 'Scramble for Africa'?
explanation: Organised by German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck, the Berlin Conference regulated European colonisation in Africa.

text: Which international organisation was established after the First World War to preserve world peace?
explanation: The League of Nations was founded in 1920 under the Treaty of Versailles and was eventually replaced by the United Nations.

text: Which celebrated Byzantine general was commissioned by Emperor Justinian I to reconquer North Africa and Italy?
explanation: Belisarius was the leading general who reconquered Vandal North Africa in 533 AD and parts of Italy for the Byzantine Empire.

text: Which Russian Tsar founded Saint Petersburg and made it the new capital of his empire?
explanation: Peter the Great founded Saint Petersburg in 1703, moving the capital from Moscow to modernise and Europeanise Russia.

text: Which Saadi military commander led the Moroccan expedition across the Sahara to conquer the Songhai Empire in 1591?
explanation: Judar Pasha led the Saadi army to a decisive victory at the Battle of Tondibi in 1591 under Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur.

text: Which Roman emperor was born in Leptis Magna (in modern-day Libya) and founded the Severan dynasty?
explanation: Septimius Severus was born in Leptis Magna in 145 AD and ruled the Roman Empire from 193 until his death in 211 AD.

text: Which Visigothic king was defeated and killed at the Battle of Guadalete in 711 by the forces of Tariq ibn Ziyad?
explanation: King Roderic fell at the Battle of Guadalete, which triggered the rapid Umayyad conquest of Hispania.

text: Which caliph led the Umayyad faction to victory at the Battle of Marj Rahit in 684 AD?
explanation: Marwan I defeated the Zubayrid loyalists at Marj Rahit, establishing the Marwanid line of the Umayyad Caliphate.

text: Which Maliki theologian and reformer is regarded as the religious founder of the Almoravid movement?
explanation: Abdallah ibn Yasin preached religious revival among the Sanhaja Berbers, establishing the ideological base of the Almoravid Empire.

text: Which Holy Roman Emperor promulgated the Golden Bull of 1356, establishing the electoral system of the empire?
explanation: Emperor Charles IV issued the Golden Bull of 1356, formalising the college of seven Prince-electors to choose the Emperor.

text: Which Abbasid caliph ordered the assassination by poison of Idris I, founder of the Idrisid dynasty, in 791 AD?
explanation: Harun al-Rashid sent an agent named al-Shammakh to poison Idris I in Morocco, fearing the growth of an Alid rival state.

text: Which renowned Mongol general orchestrated the devastating tactical victory at the Battle of Mohi in 1241 against Hungary?
explanation: Subutai planned the brilliant encirclement at Mohi that crushed the army of King Bela IV of Hungary.

text: Which Byzantine emperor forced Bohemond I of Antioch to sign the Treaty of Devol in 1108?
explanation: Alexios I Komnenos compelled Bohemond to acknowledge Byzantine suzerainty over the Principality of Antioch.

text: Which Umayyad general led the campaign against the Berber queen Dihya (the Kahina) in North Africa?
explanation: Hassan ibn al-Nu'man was initially defeated by Dihya but returned to defeat her forces definitively around 702 AD.

text: What was the original birth name of the famous Ming dynasty admiral Zheng He?
explanation: Zheng He was born Ma He into a Yunnanese Muslim family before being recruited into the imperial court.

text: Which city did the Abbasid Caliph Al-Mu'tasim construct in 836 AD to serve as his new capital?
explanation: Al-Mu'tasim founded Samarra and moved his court and Turkic military regiments there from Baghdad.

text: Which Polish king led the decisive cavalry charge that lifted the Ottoman Siege of Vienna in 1683?
explanation: John III Sobieski led the famous charge of the Winged Hussars, decisively defeating the Ottoman siege forces.

text: In which year was the Bohemian religious reformer Jan Hus executed at the stake during the Council of Constance?
explanation: Jan Hus was burned at the stake for heresy in Constance on 6 July 1415, triggering the Hussite Wars.

text: Which monarch founded the expansionist Songhai Empire and captured the city of Timbuktu in 1468?
explanation: Sonni Ali Ber ruled from 1464 to 1492, seizing Timbuktu from the Tuareg and establishing the Songhai Empire.

text: Which Achaemenid king commissioned the famous multilingual Behistun Inscription in modern-day Iran?
explanation: Darius I the Great ordered the Behistun Inscription to chronicle his accession to the throne and quell uprisings.

text: In which year was the Battle of Sagrajas (Zallaqa) fought, where the Almoravids crushed the Castilian army?
explanation: In 1086, Yusuf ibn Tashfin led the Almoravid army across the Straits to defeat King Alfonso VI of Castile.

text: Who was the only female monarch to rule the Delhi Sultanate in her own right (1236–1240)?
explanation: Razia Sultana was chosen by her father Iltutmish as heir and ruled Delhi in her own right until overthrown in 1240.

text: Which King of Portugal perished at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir (Battle of the Three Kings) in Morocco in 1578?
explanation: King Sebastian died at Alcácer Quibir without an heir, leading directly to the 60-year Iberian Union with Spain.

text: Which Umayyad caliph Arabised the state administration and minted the first purely Islamic gold dinar?
explanation: Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan replaced foreign coinage with aniconic Arabic dinars and established Arabic in state bureaux.

text: Which decisive 1600 battle paved the way for the establishment of the Tokugawa Shogunate in Japan?
explanation: Tokugawa Ieyasu's victory at Sekigahara in October 1600 unified Japan and began over 250 years of Tokugawa rule.

text: Which Roman consul was killed alongside tens of thousands of legionaries at the Battle of Cannae in 216 BC?
explanation: Lucius Aemilius Paullus died in Hannibal's double-envelopment at Cannae, whereas his co-consul Varro escaped.

text: Which Fatimid general conquered Egypt in 969 AD and founded both the city of Cairo and al-Azhar Mosque?
explanation: Jawhar al-Siqilli conquered Egypt on behalf of Caliph al-Mu'izz, immediately laying the foundations of Cairo and al-Azhar.

text: During the reign of which Seljuk Sultan was the famous vizier Nizam al-Mulk assassinated by the Hashashin in 1092?
explanation: Nizam al-Mulk was murdered in October 1092 while travelling in the company of Sultan Malik-Shah I, who died weeks later.

text: Which Marinid sultan conquered Marrakech in 1269, bringing a definitive end to the Almohad Empire?
explanation: Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Abd al-Haqq captured Marrakech in 1269, terminating Almohad rule and establishing the Marinid Sultanate.

text: In which month of the French Republican Calendar was Maximilien Robespierre overthrown and guillotined in 1794?
explanation: Robespierre fell on 9 Thermidor Year II (27 July 1794), marking the end of the Reign of Terror.

text: Which Byzantine emperor recovered the True Cross from the Sasanian Empire after defeating them in 628 AD?
explanation: Heraclius routed Khosrow II's forces and personally returned the True Cross to Jerusalem in 630 AD.

text: Which Neo-Assyrian king assembled the vast royal library of cuneiform clay tablets at Nineveh?
explanation: Ashurbanipal collected thousands of texts, including the Epic of Gilgamesh, for his great library at Nineveh.

text: The Fourth Fitna (809–813 AD) in the Abbasid Caliphate was fought between which two royal brothers?
explanation: The civil war between Harun al-Rashid's sons ended with the brutal siege of Baghdad and the execution of al-Amin.

text: The 1648 Peace of Westphalia treaties were negotiated and signed in Münster and which other German city?
explanation: Protagonists met separately due to religious rivalries: Catholics in Münster and Protestants in Osnabrück.

text: Which Grand Master of the Knights Hospitaller surrendered Rhodes to Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent in 1522?
explanation: Philippe Villiers de L'Isle-Adam defended Rhodes heroically for months before negotiating terms and eventually relocating to Malta.

text: In which year was the Battle of Marj al-Saffar (Shaqhab) fought, ending Mongol invasions of the Levant?
explanation: In 1303, the Mamluk army defeated the Ilkhanate Mongols near Damascus, halting Mongol westward incursions for good.

text: Which papal bull was issued by Pope Alexander VI in 1493, dividing newly discovered lands between Spain and Portugal?
explanation: The bull 'Inter caetera' set a meridian giving Spain claim to the west, later renegotiated in the Treaty of Tordesillas.

text: Which King of France took part in the Siege of Acre during the Third Crusade alongside Richard the Lionheart?
explanation: Philip II Augustus helped capture Acre in 1191 before returning home to France due to poor health and political rivalry.

text: Which Grand Vizier appointed in 1656 initiated the influential Köprülü era of administrative reforms in the Ottoman Empire?
explanation: Köprülü Mehmed Pasha took office on condition of absolute authority, restoring central governance after decades of court intrigue.

text: Which Almohad Caliph was defeated by the Christian coalition at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212?
explanation: Muhammad al-Nasir suffered a catastrophic defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa, which broke Almohad hegemony in Iberia.

text: Which decisive 1645 battle of the English Civil War saw the New Model Army shatter the main Royalist force?
explanation: The New Model Army, led by Fairfax and Cromwell, routed King Charles I's main army at the Battle of Naseby.

text: Which Hittite king concluded the famous Treaty of Kadesh, the earliest known peace treaty, with Pharaoh Ramesses II?
explanation: Hattusili III agreed to the Treaty of Kadesh around 1259 BC, establishing mutual non-aggression with Ramesses II.

text: In which year was the Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba officially dissolved, giving rise to the Taifa period?
explanation: In 1031, Córdoba's notables formally deposed Hisham III and abolished the caliphate, splitting Al-Andalus into Taifas.

text: Which 843 AD treaty divided the Frankish Carolingian Empire between the three grandsons of Charlemagne?
explanation: The Treaty of Verdun partitioned Charlemagne's empire among Lothair I, Louis the German, and Charles the Bald.

text: Which Abbasid Caliph developed and championed the House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma) in Baghdad?
explanation: Al-Ma'mun gave massive royal sponsorship to the House of Wisdom, accelerating the translation movement into Arabic.

text: Which city served as the imperial capital for the Western Han and Tang dynasties and eastern terminus of the Silk Road?
explanation: Chang'an (modern-day Xi'an) was one of the world's most populous cities and the eastern gateway of the Silk Road.

text: Which Byzantine emperor was overthrown by Alexios I Komnenos in 1081 when he seized the imperial throne?
explanation: Nikephoros III was forced to abdicate and become a monk when Alexios Komnenos took Constantinople in 1081.

text: Which treaty concluded in 1192 between Saladin and Richard the Lionheart ended the Third Crusade?
explanation: The Treaty of Ramla retained Muslim control over Jerusalem while permitting unarmed Christian pilgrims to visit holy sites.

text: Which Almohad ruler commissioned the Hassan Tower in Rabat and oversaw the peak of Almohad architectural glory?
explanation: Abu Yusuf Yaqub al-Mansur commissioned the massive Hassan Tower in Rabat, the Giralda in Seville, and the Koutoubia.

text: Who was the first Russian ruler to be officially crowned with the title 'Tsar of All Russia' in 1547?
explanation: Ivan IV ('Ivan the Terrible') was formally crowned the first Tsar of All Russia at the Cathedral of the Dormition.

text: In which year did the famous Battle of Kadesh take place between Ancient Egypt and the Hittite Empire?
explanation: Fought in 1274 BC between Ramesses II and Muwatalli II, Kadesh remains history's largest recorded chariot engagement.

text: Which Saadi sultan expelled the Portuguese from Agadir in 1541 and consolidated Saadi control over Morocco?
explanation: Mohammed ash-Sheikh seized Santa Cruz (Agadir) from the Portuguese in 1541, solidifying the Saadi dynasty's rule.

text: Which 732 AD battle halted the northward advance of the Umayyad army led by Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi?
explanation: Charles Martel defeated the Umayyad forces at the Battle of Tours (Poitiers), where al-Ghafiqi was killed.

text: Which Sasanian King of Kings captured Roman Emperor Valerian alive at the Battle of Edessa in 260 AD?
explanation: Shapur I captured Emperor Valerian at Edessa, marking the only time a Roman emperor was taken prisoner by a foreign enemy.

text: Which Umayyad prince escaped the Abbasid purge and founded the independent Emirate of Córdoba in 756 AD?
explanation: Nicknamed 'the Falcon of Quraysh', Abd al-Rahman I survived the slaughter of his family and created the Umayyad realm in Iberia.

text: What is the capital of Egypt?
explanation: Cairo is the capital and largest city of Egypt, known as the city of a thousand minarets.

text: Which sea separates Europe from Africa?
explanation: The Mediterranean Sea separates Europe from Africa and connects to the Atlantic Ocean via the Strait of Gibraltar.

text: Which strait connects the Mediterranean Sea to the Atlantic Ocean?
explanation: The Strait of Gibraltar separates Morocco from Spain and connects the Mediterranean to the Atlantic.

text: What is the capital of Saudi Arabia?
explanation: Riyadh is the capital and largest city of Saudi Arabia, situated in the centre of the Arabian Peninsula.

text: Which ocean separates Africa from the Americas?
explanation: The Atlantic Ocean is the second-largest ocean on Earth and separates the Americas from Europe and Africa.

text: What is the capital of Japan?
explanation: Tokyo is the capital of Japan and one of the most populous urban centres in the world.

text: On which continent are the Atlas Mountains located?
explanation: The Atlas Mountains span across Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia in north-western Africa.

text: What is the capital of Algeria?
explanation: Algiers is the capital and largest city of Algeria, situated on the Mediterranean coast.

text: Which artificial canal connects the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea?
explanation: The Suez Canal in Egypt is a crucial waterway that allows ships to travel directly between Europe and Asia.

text: What is the capital of Tunisia?
explanation: Tunis is the capital and largest city of Tunisia, located near the ancient site of Carthage.

text: Which mountain range forms a natural border between France and Spain?
explanation: The Pyrenees form a natural boundary separating the Iberian Peninsula from France.

text: What is the capital of Italy?
explanation: Rome is the capital of Italy and contains the Vatican City within its borders.

text: Which famous river flows through Baghdad, the capital of Iraq?
explanation: The Tigris flows through Baghdad and converges with the Euphrates to form the Shatt al-Arab.

text: What is the capital of the United Kingdom?
explanation: London is the capital of the United Kingdom, situated along the River Thames.

text: On which continent is Brazil located?
explanation: Brazil is the largest country in South America by both land area and population.

text: What is the capital of Spain?
explanation: Madrid is the capital and largest city of Spain, located in the centre of the Iberian Peninsula.

text: Which continent lies directly to the east of the Red Sea?
explanation: The Red Sea separates the continent of Africa to the west from Asia to the east.

text: What is the capital of Jordan?
explanation: Amman is the capital and largest city of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan.

text: What is the world's largest island by surface area?
explanation: Greenland is the largest non-continental island on Earth and is an autonomous territory of Denmark.

text: What is the capital of Lebanon?
explanation: Beirut is the capital and largest city of Lebanon, situated on the Mediterranean coast.

text: Which river flows through the city of Paris?
explanation: The River Seine flows through Paris, dividing the city into the Right Bank and Left Bank.

text: What is the capital of Germany?
explanation: Berlin is the capital and most populous city of Germany.

text: Which Asian nation is widely known as the 'Land of the Rising Sun'?
explanation: Japan's name translates literally to 'sun origin', giving rise to this famous nickname.

text: What is the capital of the United Arab Emirates?
explanation: Abu Dhabi is the capital of the United Arab Emirates and the largest emirate by land area.

text: What is the highest mountain peak in Morocco and North Africa?
explanation: Mount Toubkal stands at 4,167 metres in the High Atlas range of Morocco.

text: What is the capital of Turkey?
explanation: Ankara has been Turkey's capital since 1923, whilst Istanbul remains its largest city.

text: The famous Niagara Falls are situated on the border between Canada and which other country?
explanation: Niagara Falls straddles the border between the Canadian province of Ontario and New York State.

text: What is the capital of the Republic of Iraq?
explanation: Baghdad is the capital and largest city of Iraq, founded during the Abbasid Caliphate.

text: What is the Dead Sea particularly famous for?
explanation: The Dead Sea is nearly ten times saltier than the ocean, which prevents complex organisms from living in it.

text: What is the capital of Qatar?
explanation: Doha is the capital and main economic centre of the State of Qatar, located on the Persian Gulf.

text: Which European country is shaped distinctly like a boot on a map?
explanation: The Italian Peninsula has a distinctive boot shape protruding into the Mediterranean Sea.

text: What is the capital of the Sultanate of Oman?
